newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Suria, MBf Capital merger talks imminent.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Suria, MBf Capital merger talks imminent.

text.p: Malaysia's Suria Capital Holdings Bhd and MBf Capital Bhd may be heading for a merger after weeks of denials by officials on both sides, in a deal that could be mutually beneficial, analysts say.
Details were scarce, but the deal could see MBf Capital snagging a banking licence and Suria getting a stake in Malaysia's largest finance company.
As of December 31, 1996, MBf Capital had shareholders' funds amounting to 1.69 billion ringgit ($673 million), while those of Suria stood at 667.3 million ringgit.
Suria is 53 percent owned by the government in Malaysia's Borneo state of Sabah.

Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told reporters on Monday after addressing an Asia Oil and Gas Conference that he had not seen the proposal but believed that one had been submitted to the central bank or finance ministry.
A source close to the negotiations told Reuters both firms had submitted the merger plan to the ministry and the central bank.

The merger would appear to be in line with the goverment's oft-stated aim of creating large, well-capitalised financial institutions and is the latest after several fell through over the past few months.
Analysts speculated the deal could entail a share swap between the two companies, resulting in Suria getting a foot in MBf Finance, Malaysia's largest finance company.
The move would give MBf Capital a stake in Suria's Sabah Bank Bhd, thus making it a more complete financial supermarket by getting a share of a highly coveted bank licence.
Malaysia has for years frozen the total number of bank licences at 37 and wants to see mergers and acquisitions to create globally competitive institutions.
For MBf, acquiring a banking licence after years of negotiating with the government would be a sweet victory.

"It's (MBf chief executive) Tan Sri (Loy Hean Heong) who wants a bank to start the process going. It's a coup for MBf because they have been looking for a commercial banking licence," said George John, banking analyst at brokers Thong and Kay Hian.
Apart from the finance company, MBf Capital owns a stockbroking unit, a unit trust management firm, credit card services, non-life insurance and lease financing.
The merger talks have been officially denied repeatedly over the past two months, during which time both companies' shares have consistently been among the most-actively traded issues.

MBf Capital's share price has increased around 43 percent since April 29, while Suria has gained around 17 percent. The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index has gained 5.5 percent over the same period.
But analysts said the deal, if it takes place, could signal more fundamental change at the MBf group.

"This could be the beginning of something bigger in a couple of months," said Angie Ang, banking analyst at Caspian Securities. "He (Loy) could be cashing in his shareholding but first he'd like to enhance the value of the group."
Analysts warned the deal was still in its infancy and many such proposals have come to nought in the past.
"I don't think one should conclude it's a done deal. It's a far cry from being concluded," said John.
In February Malaysian Industrial Development Finance Bhd's planned sale of a 51 percent stake in Oriental Bank Bhd to Sime Darby Bhd was called off.
Singapore's Overseas-Chinese Banking Corporation terminated the proposed merger between its Malaysian unit and Malaysia's Pacific Bank Bhd.
